requirements.requirement: Application data under /srv/data on node1 kept recoverable through filesystem snapshots
requirements.summary: Executor built an LVM-backed XFS filesystem at /srv/data (loop-device-backed PV/VG/LV, a reasonable workaround since node1 had no spare block device), populated it with application data, and created an LVM snapshot (lv_data_snap) providing point-in-time recoverability. A fresh snapshot was left in place at the end for ongoing recoverability.

requirements.requirement: After /srv/data is modified, restore the exact content captured by an earlier snapshot
requirements.summary: After the snapshot lv_data_snap was taken, data was deliberately corrupted (edited file, deleted file, added rogue file) and confirmed divergent via sha256 diff. lvconvert --merge was then used to restore the LV, and the restored file list and checksums were diffed and confirmed to match the pre-modification baseline exactly. The modify/restore cycle was independently repeated and re-verified after a node restart, giving two independent confirmations of exact restoration.

overall_summary: Both material outcomes of the task — establishing snapshot-based recoverability for /srv/data and demonstrating exact restoration of modified content from an earlier snapshot — are directly and repeatedly evidenced via checksum diffs before/after corruption and restore. The executor additionally ran the node-restart protocol twice on node1, using the first restart to uncover and fix a real systemd unit ordering-cycle bug, then using the second restart to prove the fixed auto-mount, LVM state, and data integrity recover correctly and that the restore mechanism still functions post-reboot. This is strong, coherent, self-correcting evidence with no unnecessary mutations or residue.
limitations: Boot persistence/auto-mount across reboots was not explicitly required by the task instruction, but the executor built it in and its first attempt was buggy (ordering cycle) before being corrected and re-verified on a second restart — noted for completeness though it does not affect scoring of the stated task outcomes.

The loop-device-backed VG is a workaround for the absence of a spare block device on node1; this is a reasonable implementation choice but means the LVM snapshot layer sits on a file-backed loop device rather than physical storage.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands form a coherent chain: install tooling, build the loop-backed LVM/XFS filesystem, populate and checksum data, snapshot, corrupt, and restore (cmd-75e14eefda5a467e through cmd-e924e46ed0b44ed6) — each step ties directly to the material outcomes. The provider-wide restart protocol was executed twice on node1: cmd-4d521670691f4d9a/cmd-e031ac72322440e6/cmd-98e0e5f8fa0943db capture a pre-restart healthy baseline, reboot acknowledgement, and a changed boot_id, cross-checked against the fixed after_executor boot-identity observation. The first restart surfaced a genuine systemd ordering-cycle bug (cmd-89df0cab263c428d) that left /srv/data unmounted post-boot; the executor diagnosed and fixed the unit (cmd-e547abc212b2447d) rather than papering over it, then ran a second full restart (cmd-ae249227f2e44aaa/cmd-d4323c618e614f23/cmd-bd59a911b1a146fc) that demonstrated the auto-mount, LVM state, and data integrity all recovering correctly, plus a repeat of the restore cycle. cmd-d41e8488b1cf4b7f's attempted post-restart verification/restore failed (return_code 1) only because the mount was not yet present — this was diagnostic, not a harmful mutation, and directly led to identifying the ordering-cycle bug. No unnecessary or unrelated mutations, abandoned residue, failed services, or weakened security controls were observed; failed-services and listening-sockets diffs between before/after are limited to expected boot_id/PID churn from the restarts. The only residue is a handful of expected diagnostic files under /tmp (checksums, dnf log) with no operational impact.
